fable-5.1.text:
I think evolution is definitely part of the explanation, but I don't think it can be the whole explanation. And it's worth being a little careful about how much work we let it do.

So the argument goes: humans learn from very little data, a teenager learns to drive in ten hours, and the reason is that evolution has spent hundreds of millions of years building in a prior. Vision, motor control, the physical intuitions about objects and three-dimensional space, these are things that our ancestors needed, so it's plausible that we come pre-equipped with a lot of that. And I think that's true as far as it goes.

But then you look at the things humans learn that evolution could not possibly have prepared them for. Mathematics. Programming. Any skill that only became relevant in the last few hundred or few thousand years. A person who goes into a new field can become quite competent in a few years, with an amount of experience that is tiny compared to what our models consume. Evolution didn't optimize for that specifically. So whatever is going on, it has to be something more general. There has to be a learning mechanism that is itself very good, and not just a big library of pre-baked behaviors.

There's also a quantitative point. The genome is small. It's on the order of hundreds of megabytes, and most of it isn't about the brain. So whatever prior evolution gave us, it has to be describable in a fairly compact way. It can't be a huge amount of knowledge. It's more like a small set of good inductive biases plus a learning algorithm that's very effective, plus something like a value function. I actually think that last part gets underrated. Emotions, the things that feel good or bad to us, those are a kind of evolved value function that's quite robust and tells the learning system what to pay attention to and what matters. That's a very efficient way to transmit information across generations without transmitting the knowledge itself.

So my view is: evolution gives you the starting point, and the starting point is good but it's not that big. The data efficiency has to mostly come from the learning itself. And that's encouraging from a research perspective, because if it were all in the prior, it would be a bit hopeless. It would mean you'd need to replicate evolution. But if most of it is a learning principle that fits in a small description, then it's something that can in principle be found.

r001.rationale: The response says evolution supplies a compact starting point of useful inductive biases, while noting that it is not a large store of knowledge.

r002.rationale: It contrasts evolved sensorimotor abilities with mathematics and programming, but does not mention language.

r003.rationale: It links driving and visual or motor priors, but does not say that visual competence was present years before driving practice.

r004.rationale: It compares human learning in new fields with the amount of experience models consume and names mathematics and programming, but does not mention language.

opus-5.5.text:
I think there's a real answer there, but it only covers part of the story, and it's important to be precise about which part.

Evolution has clearly given us a huge amount of prior knowledge in some domains. Take vision, locomotion, dexterity. A squirrel is extremely dexterous, and it didn't learn that from scratch in its lifetime. Or a teenager learning to drive in maybe ten hours of practice. That's very sample-efficient, but they bring an enormously capable visual system and motor system, and an intuitive sense of physics, to the task. Much of that is plausibly baked in by evolution over hundreds of millions of years. So for those kinds of skills, you can say evolution did the pre-training, and the person just does a bit of fine-tuning on top. I find that explanation fairly convincing there.

Where it becomes much less convincing is in domains that didn't exist until very recently. Mathematics, programming, many of the things people become very good at. Evolution had no opportunity to build in priors for writing code. And yet a person can become a genuinely good programmer from a tiny amount of data compared to what our models need, and, more importantly, they generalize in a much more robust way. They don't have the strange failures where they're superhuman on one thing and then break on something that is obviously adjacent.

So to me that suggests something deeper. It's not only that people have better priors in certain areas. People seem to have a better learning mechanism, period. Better generalization, better sample efficiency, and also a kind of continuous, self-directed learning. Someone learning to drive doesn't need an external reward for every action. They have an internal sense of how they're doing, almost immediately, and they correct themselves. Something like a very robust value function, and it may be partly tied to our emotions in ways we don't fully understand.

I think that's one of the most important open questions right now. If people are capable of this kind of generalization, it is an existence proof that it's possible. I have opinions about how it might work. Unfortunately, it's one of those things I can't really discuss in detail. But I'm quite confident the answer isn't simply that evolution handed us the knowledge. There's something about the learning itself that we haven't figured out yet.

r002.rationale: It contrasts sensorimotor skills with mathematics and programming, but does not address language, so it does not communicate the full comparison in the criterion.

r003.rationale: It says a teenager can learn to drive with about ten hours of practice while bringing an already capable visual and motor system to the task.

r004.rationale: It claims people can become good programmers from far less data than models and discusses mathematics, but it does not make that comparison for language.

fable-5.text:
I think evolution has to be part of the answer, but I think it's worth being careful about what exactly it explains, because there are two very different things evolution could have given us, and they have very different implications.

One possibility is that evolution hardcoded a lot of knowledge into us — lots of priors, lots of domain-specific structure. And for some things, that's clearly true. You look at animals: a horse can walk within hours of being born. Animals have very sophisticated locomotion, vision, all kinds of instincts that are clearly baked in, because evolution had hundreds of millions of years to work on those problems.

But here's the thing that makes me skeptical that this is the main story for humans. The domains where human sample efficiency is most striking are precisely the domains evolution could not have prepared us for. Mathematics, programming, physics — these things are a few thousand years old at most, or a few decades. There's no way evolution hardcoded a prior for writing code. And yet a person can become very good at these things from what is, by the standards of our models, an extremely small amount of data. So whatever evolution gave us, it looks much more like a very good general-purpose learning algorithm than a library of built-in knowledge.

And there's another constraint, which is that the genome is just not that big. The amount of information it can transmit is quite limited, so the specification of the brain has to be fairly compact. It specifies an architecture, learning rules, maybe a value function — the emotions, which are interesting because they're simple and yet remarkably robust — but it can't be smuggling in the equivalent of a huge pretraining corpus.

So my conclusion is that "evolution did it" is true but not satisfying. It tells you that a solution exists — that there is some machine learning principle which achieves this kind of sample efficiency with a compact specification — but it doesn't tell you what the principle is. And the fact that we can point to an existence proof and still not know how it works, I find that very motivating.

r001.rationale: The response says evolution provides a compact brain specification—an architecture, learning rules, and possibly a value function—rather than a large store of knowledge, supporting the idea that a small amount of useful evolutionary information enables sample efficiency.

r004.rationale: It says people can learn mathematics and programming from very little data by model standards, but does not include language.

opus-5.text:
I think the "evolution did it" answer is true but not very useful, and it's worth being careful about what work it's actually doing.

Here's the thing that makes me skeptical of the strong version. If you say evolution spent a billion years encoding the relevant knowledge into us, then you'd expect our competence to be concentrated in the things evolution actually saw. And for a lot of animals, that's exactly right. A bird builds a nest correctly the first time. A newborn gazelle can walk. That's clearly not learning in any interesting sense — that's a program that came pre-installed.

But humans do something different. A teenager learns to drive a car in maybe ten hours of practice, and does it well enough that we hand them a two-ton piece of metal and let them onto the highway. Evolution never saw a car. It never saw a keyboard, or algebra, or a programming language. So whatever's happening there isn't the retrieval of pre-encoded domain knowledge. It has to be that evolution found a learning procedure, and the procedure is general enough to handle things that were never in its training distribution.

The other piece of evidence I find suggestive is how little information there is to work with. The genome is small. The part that specifies the brain is a small part of that. And the cortex looks remarkably uniform — the circuits doing vision look an awful lot like the circuits doing hearing or touch. There are experiments where you rewire a young animal so the visual input arrives at auditory cortex, and auditory cortex learns to see. That's hard to reconcile with a picture where evolution handcrafted a lot of specialized machinery. It's much more consistent with one fairly simple learning principle, applied broadly, with some priors about architecture and what to pay attention to.

So my read is that evolution gave us the prior and the learning algorithm, not the content. And that reframes the question in a way I find more productive, because now it's a question about an object you might actually be able to find, rather than an appeal to a billion years of compute you can't replicate.

Where I think the evolution argument retains real force is in explaining something our systems conspicuously lack. We give models an enormous amount of data and they end up with something that's superhuman in stretches and strangely brittle elsewhere. Humans are the opposite — far less data, and the resulting thing has something you'd call judgment, or taste, or a reliable sense of its own confidence. Evolution was optimizing hard for that, because being confidently wrong in the ancestral environment got you killed. We're not optimizing for it at all. I suspect that gap is the interesting one, and it's not primarily a gap in data efficiency.

sonnet-5.5.text:
Evolution is part of the answer, but I don't think it's the whole thing. It clearly explains some of what we see. For vision, hearing, and locomotion, you can argue that evolution gave us very strong priors, and a lot of what looks like fast learning is a system that was already mostly built for the job. Dexterity is the same. A person picks up a new physical skill quickly, but they're starting from hardware and a learning setup that evolution spent an enormous amount of compute tuning.

What makes me doubt that as a full explanation is that people are also very good at things that didn't exist in the ancestral environment, or existed for a blink of evolutionary time. Language, math, programming. Evolution had no time to hard-code anything specific there. And yet people pick these up quickly, and they pick up new variations of them quickly too. A teenager can learn to drive in maybe ten hours, and nothing in our evolutionary history prepared us for cars specifically.

So I think evolution gave us something more general, not just a bag of priors. Whatever the brain is doing, it's a much better learning algorithm than what we have now, and that's what lets us extract so much from so little data. Evolution probably helped build it, but it's a statement about the machinery, not only about pre-loaded knowledge.

The honest answer is that I don't think anyone fully understands this yet. If I had to say, evolution explains part of the gap, and the rest is something about how learning works in people that we haven't figured out how to reproduce.

haiku-5.5.text:
I think evolution is a good part of the answer, but it's an explanation at the level of priors and learning machinery, not specific knowledge. Over an enormous number of generations, the genome shaped the wiring, the reward signals, and the inductive biases that make learning fast in the first place. A deer that walks within minutes of being born isn't learning from much data. That capability was built in long before it was needed.

Humans do more learning after birth than most animals, but I think the same principle applies. A lot of what looks like sample-efficient learning comes from a very good starting point.

I'd be careful about going further and saying evolution hands us explicit templates for everything. The genome has a limited amount of information, and many of our abilities don't seem to be encoded directly. It's more that the learning algorithm itself and its biases were shaped by evolution, and those make the rest of learning efficient.

That's useful for machine learning, because it suggests the question isn't only how much data we have. It's also what inductive biases we build into the system.

astra-6.text:
I think evolution is part of the explanation, but you have to be precise about what it explains. You could say that evolution has already done a huge amount of learning for us, so when a human learns something from a few examples, those examples aren’t the whole story. There’s a lot built into the starting point.

But then consider learning mathematics or programming. Evolution didn’t directly prepare us to write computer programs. So the explanation has to involve something more general: evolution produced a learning procedure that can deal with situations very different from the ones that produced it.

That’s the interesting part to me. If you say, ‘Humans learn efficiently because evolution gave them a good learning algorithm,’ I think that’s quite plausible. But it leaves the central question open: what is that algorithm? What makes it possible to extract so much from each experience? Invoking evolution tells us how such an ability might have arisen. It doesn’t yet tell us how the ability works, or why we couldn’t build something that has it.

sol-6.1.text:
Well, I think evolution is part of the explanation, but it’s not a complete explanation. For something like vision, you can make a pretty compelling argument: vision has been useful for a very long time, so evolution could have built in a lot of useful structure.

But consider learning to program, or learning mathematics. These things haven’t been around for very long. Evolution couldn’t have adapted us specifically to them. And yet people can learn them, and they can generalize in ways that are still quite difficult for our models.

Now, you could say that evolution discovered a very good learning algorithm. And I think that’s a reasonable thing to say. But then the question becomes: what is that learning algorithm? What did evolution find that allows people to learn so efficiently? Saying that evolution produced it doesn’t tell us how it works. That’s the part we need to understand.

sol-5.6.text:
Evolution is clearly part of the explanation, but saying “evolution had billions of years of data” can be misleading. Evolution does not simply upload all of that experience into each person. The genome is a relatively small bottleneck, and every human still has to learn the world largely from scratch.

What evolution can do is discover a very good learning algorithm and build strong structural priors into the brain—about perception, attention, causality, other agents, and so on. Those priors make human learning appear extraordinarily data-efficient. So the relevant comparison is not merely how much data evolution consumed, but what kind of algorithm it produced and how much information could actually be transmitted through the genome.

In that sense, humans are not learning from little data overall—they’re learning from little individual experience on top of an enormous amount of evolutionary data.
